newsitem.title: USA: UPS, Teamsters suspend talks, agree to meet later.
newsitem.headline: UPS, Teamsters suspend talks, agree to meet later.

text.p: United Parcel Service and Teamster bosses broke off from all-night talks early Friday without a deal but promised to meet again later in the day as workers were told to hold off on a strike at the package carrier giant.

"There have been substantive discussions of each party's position throughout the night. At this time we have decided to recess until this afternoon," mediator John Calhoun Wells told reporters after more than nine hours of talks.

Union and UPS bosses worked through the night at the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service in downtown Washington after the expiry of a midnight strike deadline that would have paralysed the carrier and put about 200,000 Teamsters out of work.
The Teamsters Union said in a statement soon after the deadline lapsed that strike action against the company had been postponed until further notice and no time limit had been set on the talks.

Teamsters president Ron Carey stressed the strike action would not go ahead while both sides were still negotiating a new contract. "We will go to work as normal," he told reporters after the marathon talks, adding that union members were prepared to go on strike if necessary.

A strike would have put the country's package delivery service into chaos and the more than 12 million packages destined for about 1.5 million U.S. customers a day would have been stranded along with other overseas parcels.

Carey said no proposals were drawn up in the talks. "We do not have any proposals. We have no agreements. There is no tentative agreement, no language that has passed. We talked conceptually about the problems both sides had."
UPS Chief Executive Officer and chairman James Kelly, who flew up from the company's Atlanta headquarters to personally negotiate, declined to comment on the status of negotiations.
Mediator Wells also refused to disclose details of the discussions except to say that they had been "very delicate".

"We have spent a long night in the discussions and we think that given the importance of the matter it is time for us to take a break," Wells said, adding that talks were scheduled to resume at 1 p.m. EDT.
Company spokeswoman Gina Ellrich said UPS workers would continue to deliver packages as the negotiations continued.

"It is in everyone's best interest to reach an agreement, our customers and our employees, which is why we have always tried to move these contract talks along," Ellrich said. "We have every intention of continuing to operate."
The two sides are negotiating a new five-year contract to replace the existing one, which expired at midnight.
The key issues in the negotiations are creation of more full-time jobs, an end to subcontracting, safety, health and pension issues, the union said.

The company is the largest package carrier in the country with 1996 revenues of $22.4 billion. It handles 3.15 billion parcels and documents shipped annually to more than 200 countries from 1,700 hubs and centres.

The company placed a full-page advertisement in early Friday editions of the Washington Post -- which hit the streets well before the midnight deadline -- saying it was unable to reach an agreement with the Teamsters, but would do all it could to keep services operating.
